name: Vivid Purple
lede: Vivid Purple is a fully saturated screen violet that appears in several color lists, and a reminder that paint and dye struggle to reach it.

sections.title: One name, several lists
sections.body:
Vivid Purple is the name of a block in the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary gives the same name with a first record in 1919 [1]. A web survey also named a color this purple, and Wikipedia's entry cites the ISCC-NBS source [1]. Three near-twins sit within about two and a half units of the swatch: Veronica, [[electric-violet]] and [[vivid-violet]] [1].

The swatch is more intense than almost any named purple. Its chroma is about 120, near the top of what a screen can show, where a muted purple such as [[royal-purple]] sits far lower [1].

sections.title: Hard to mix, easy to light
sections.body:
A teaching book on color notes that mixing a vivid purple from red and blue paint, ink or dye is frustrating, because the traditional red-yellow-blue primaries cover a reduced range of colors, especially between red and blue [2]. This swatch is a screen color made with light, so it lies outside what most pigments can make [2][1].

The dyers' vivid purple is a different thing. When Finlay watched chemists reproduce Tyrian purple, the cloth came out as bright as anything Perkin made [3]. Another book lists a gold-and-aluminium compound, nicknamed purple plague, that shows a vivid purple [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our archive of 23,781 has a color within six units of this one covering five per cent of the canvas [5]. The photographs are of aged, varnished paintings, which dull saturated colors further [5]. The nearest named colors are [[blue-violet]] and plain [[violet]] [1].
